app.title: CDFuse — NetCDF comparison
app.summary: A person uploads a candidate gridded dataset and a reference dataset, or loads a demonstration pair, and can add a study-area boundary. They then choose the variable in each file and confirm which coordinates hold time, latitude and longitude. They can also set time shifts, keep one hour per day, and pick a temporal aggregation, a grid-alignment method and a set of skill metrics. Running the comparison aligns both datasets in time and on a common grid, then scores every grid cell. The person reads a summary table and one map per metric, and downloads each metric field (PNG, NetCDF, GeoTIFF, CSV), a run report that records every setting, or everything as one ZIP.

task.text: Score how well a gridded dataset reproduces a reference dataset at every grid cell, and export the metric maps with a record of the settings used.

data.text: Two gridded time series of the same variable, stored as NetCDF with time, latitude and longitude dimensions, plus an optional vector boundary polygon.
data.item: a grid cell's time series in the candidate dataset, paired with the same cell in the reference dataset

stage.text: evaluating a gridded product against a benchmark dataset, before reporting on its skill

mechanism.text: Numbered tabs take the person from loading data, to configuring coordinates, time handling, alignment and metrics, to results. A sidebar ticks off each stage as it is done. The results tab shows overview counts, a summary-statistics table and one colour-mapped grid map per metric. Each map has its own statistics and download buttons beside it.

field.text: cell-wise skill scoring of gridded datasets against a reference in the earth sciences

workflow.name: score a candidate dataset against a reference and export the results

steps.here: Separate uploaders for the candidate and reference NetCDF files, or a button that loads a synthetic demonstration pair. Optionally, a shapefile, GeoJSON or GeoPackage boundary.

steps.step: map each input's fields onto a common structure
steps.here: For each dataset, pick the variable and confirm the auto-detected time, latitude and longitude coordinates. Pick a slice for any extra dimension, and set an optional time shift in hours.

steps.step: set how the inputs are matched before computing
steps.here: Optionally keep one hour per day for each dataset and match on calendar date. Choose a temporal aggregation (daily, monthly, seasonal, annual) and its statistic, and choose whether to interpolate one grid onto the other or use only exactly shared cells.

steps.step: compute a value from the data
steps.here: Pick metrics (Correlation, NSE, KGE, PBIAS, RMSE, MAE, Bias), optionally clip to the boundary, and run. The inputs are checked first. Each metric is computed per cell over the shared time steps, and cells with too few pairs or an undefined denominator are masked.

steps.step: look over every item at a glance
steps.here: Counts of matched time steps and grid cells, an expandable list of the processing notes, and a table of the mean, median, min, max and coverage of each metric.
One map per metric, with a fixed or robust diverging colour scale, the boundary outline, guidance on interpreting the metric, and its statistics beside it.
Per-metric PNG, CF-attributed NetCDF, GeoTIFF and long-format CSV files, plus a summary CSV, a plain-text run report recording every setting, and a ZIP with all of them.

distinctive: The comparison is asymmetric: one dataset is the reference treated as truth and the other is the candidate being scored, so which one goes where changes the answer.
Metrics are computed independently at every grid cell through time. A value missing on either side drops that time step from both, and undefined cells are stored as missing, never as zero.
No product's conventions are assumed: time shifts and the choice of hour of day are explicit settings for each dataset, and longitudes and latitude order are normalised automatically.
A run report records every setting and processing note, so the comparison can be reproduced.
An optional vector boundary is drawn on every map and can mask the metric fields to the study area.
